summary: This document updates the IPv6 specification (RFC 2460) so tunnel protocols that use UDP over IPv6 can skip the UDP checksum in certain cases. This is allowed when the tunnel's header information is protected on the inner packet being carried. Skipping it avoids the computation cost and improves performance.

plainLanguage.summary: When one network carries another's traffic inside a UDP packet, the outer UDP header carries its own checksum that checks the same bytes the inner packet already checks for itself. This RFC allows a tunnel to leave that outer checksum out, under rules that limit the damage a corrupted outer header can do.

questions: can ipv6 udp checksum be zero
why do udp tunnels skip the checksum
what does rfc 6935 change in rfc 2460
subtitle: Lets a tunnel over UDP skip the checksum on its outer header when the inner packet is already checked.

tldr.problem: IPv6 requires every UDP packet to carry a checksum. A tunnel that carries packets over UDP has to compute a second checksum on its outer header, even though the packet inside already has one of its own.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC updates IPv6 so that each UDP port has a mode, and a tunnel protocol may enable a zero-checksum mode for a specific port, subject to the node and usage requirements in RFC 6936.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard published in April 2013 that has not been obsoleted or updated. It updates RFC 2460, and it applies only to tunnels: the outer packet is not protected, so the tunnel design has to tolerate misdelivery.

facts.label: Scope of the change
facts.value: A zero UDP checksum in the outer datagram of a tunnel protocol

facts.label: Default mode behaviour
facts.value: The checksum is computed, a computed zero becomes hex FFFF, and receivers discard a zero checksum by default

facts.label: Zero-checksum mode
facts.value: Enabled per port, for sending and/or receiving

facts.label: Tunnel context key
facts.value: The tunneled protocol number, the IPv6 source and destination addresses, and the UDP source and destination ports

facts.label: Companion document
facts.value: RFC 6936, the applicability statement for IPv6 UDP datagrams with zero checksums

today: RFC 6935 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2013, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. It updates RFC 2460, and the update is conditional on the node and usage requirements of RFC 6936 rather than on anything in this document alone.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This document is an update of the IPv6 specification of RFC 2460 for cases where a tunnel protocol uses UDP with IPv6 to tunnel packets.

Tunnel protocols have become increasingly important with the growth of the Internet, because they enable the deployment of new protocols. A tunnel can be deployed rapidly, while the time to upgrade and deploy a new protocol on a critical mass of routers, middleboxes and hosts on the global Internet is now measured in decades. At the same time, the increasing use of firewalls and other security-related middleboxes means that truly new tunnel protocols with new protocol numbers are unlikely to be deployable in a reasonable time frame. The result is an increasing interest in and use of UDP-based tunnel protocols. In such protocols there is an encapsulated inner packet, and the outer packet carrying the tunneled inner packet is a UDP packet, which can pass through firewalls and other middleboxes that perform the filtering that is a fact of life on the current Internet.

Tunnel endpoints may be routers or middleboxes aggregating traffic from a number of tunnel users, so the computation of an additional checksum on the outer UDP packet may be seen as an unwarranted burden on nodes that implement a tunnel protocol, especially if the inner packets are already protected by a checksum. IPv4 has a checksum over the IP packet header and the checksum on the outer UDP packet may be set to zero. IPv6 has no checksum in the IP header, and RFC 2460 explicitly states that IPv6 receivers must discard UDP packets with a zero checksum. Sending a UDP datagram with a zero checksum is permitted in IPv4 but explicitly forbidden in IPv6.

This document updates RFC 2460 to allow endpoints to use a zero UDP checksum under constrained situations, primarily for IPv6 tunnel transports that carry checksum-protected packets, following the applicability statements and constraints in RFC 6936. The advice in the unicast UDP usage guidelines for application designers of RFC 5405 is applicable, both its section on UDP tunnels and its section on the usage of checksums.

While the origin of this specification is the problem raised by the Automatic Multicast Tunnels work, the RFC expects it to have wide applicability. Since the first draft was written, the need for an efficient UDP tunneling mechanism has increased, and other IETF working groups, notably LISP and Softwires, have expressed a need to update the UDP checksum processing in RFC 2460.

The document discusses only IPv6, because the problem being addressed does not exist for IPv4, so all references to IP mean IPv6.

The terms tunneling and tunneled are used as adjectives. When the RFC refers to tunneling packets it means the outer packet header that provides the tunneling function. When it refers to tunneled packets it means the inner packet, the packet being carried in the tunnel.
sections.plainLanguage:
Tunnels exist because the equipment in the path will not understand a new protocol but will pass UDP through. The cost is that the tunnel adds a UDP header around every packet, and IPv6 insists that header has a checksum of its own. This RFC makes that checksum optional for tunnels.

The outer packet is the one the tunnel adds; the inner packet is the one the tunnel is carrying. Everything the RFC says about skipping a checksum applies to the outer packet only.

sections.title: The Cost of the Outer Checksum
sections.content: When using tunnel protocols based on UDP, there is both a benefit and a cost to computing and checking the UDP checksum of the outer encapsulating UDP transport header. In certain cases where reducing the forwarding cost is important, the cost of the computation may outweigh the benefit of the checksum. This document provides an update for usage of the UDP checksum with IPv6. The update is specified for use by a tunnel protocol that transports packets that are themselves protected by a checksum.
sections.plainLanguage: Computing and checking the checksum costs work on every packet at both ends of the tunnel. Where that work matters more than the protection, the protection can be dropped, but only when the packet inside is protected in its own way.

sections.title: Corruption in a Tunnel Context
sections.content:
The RFC sets out what a tunnel protocol has to take into account to be robust, and why the use of a zero UDP checksum is thought to be safe for deployment.

Context, that is the tunneling state, should be established by exchanging application Protocol Data Units carried in checksummed UDP datagrams, or by using other protocols that provide integrity protection against corruption. Those control packets should also carry any negotiation needed to enable the tunnel endpoint to accept UDP datagrams with a zero checksum, and identify the set of ports that are used. The control traffic has to be robust against corruption, because undetected errors can lead to long-lived and significant failures affecting much more than the single packet that was corrupted.

Keepalive datagrams with a zero UDP checksum should be sent to validate the network path, because the path between tunnel endpoints can change and the set of middleboxes along it may change during the life of an association. Paths with middleboxes that drop datagrams with a zero UDP checksum will drop these keepalives, so the keepalive traffic should include datagrams with a non-zero checksum and datagrams with a zero checksum, to let the endpoints discover and react to that behaviour in a timely way.

Receivers should attempt to detect corruption of the address information in an encapsulating packet. A robust tunnel protocol should track tunnel context based on the 5-tuple: the tunneled protocol number, the IPv6 source address, the IPv6 destination address, the UDP source port and the UDP destination port. If the datagram header matches the 5-tuple and the node has enabled zero checksum for that port, the payload is matched to the wrong context, and the tunneled packet is decapsulated and forwarded by the tunnel egress. If a corrupted datagram matches a different 5-tuple and the node has enabled zero checksum for the port, the payload is matched to the wrong context and may be processed by the wrong tunnel protocol, provided it also passes that protocol's verification. If a corrupted datagram matches a 5-tuple and the node has not enabled zero checksum for that port, the datagram is discarded.

When only the source information is corrupted, the datagram could arrive at the intended application, which will process it and try to match it against an existing tunnel context. The likelihood that a corrupted packet enters a valid context is reduced when the protocol restricts processing to only the source addresses with established contexts. When both source and destination fields are corrupted, that likelihood decreases too, except when the error replaces one packet header with another, so that both packets could be tunneled and the corrupted packet could match a previously defined context.

Receivers should also attempt to detect corruption of source-fragmented encapsulating packets, because a tunnel protocol may reassemble fragments at the wrong endpoint or in the wrong context. The IPv6 length of the encapsulating header may be checked, although RFC 6936 points out the weakness in that check, and if the encapsulated packet is protected by a transport or other checksum these errors can be detected with some probability.

Tunnel protocols using UDP have advantages over other applications that reduce the risk of a corrupted tunnel packet reaching a destination that will receive it. A tunneled packet may be forwarded to the wrong address domain, for example a private address domain where the inner packet's address is not routable, or it may fail a source address check such as Unicast Reverse Path Forwarding of RFC 2827, and be dropped. The destination address of a tunneled packet may not be reachable at all from the delivered domain, for example an Ethernet frame whose destination hardware address is not present on the LAN segment that was reached. The type of the tunneled packet may prevent delivery, because interpreting an IP packet payload as an Ethernet frame would likely result in the packet being dropped as invalid. And the tunneled packet's own checksum or integrity mechanism may detect corruption of the inner packet caused at the same time as corruption of the outer packet header, so the resulting packet would likely be dropped as invalid.
sections.plainLanguage: Without the outer checksum, a corrupted outer header could hand the inner packet to the wrong tunnel. The RFC lists the checks that catch this: the tunnel is identified by five fields, the inner packet is usually checked by its own protocol, and the inner packet's address and type are checked again after it leaves the tunnel. Together these make a misdelivery unlikely, though not impossible.

sections.title: Why Tunnels and Not Other Traffic
sections.content:
Tunnels carry inner packets that have their own semantics, which may make corruption less likely to reach the intended destination and be accepted as a valid packet. This is true for IP packets, with the addition of the verification that can be made by the tunnel protocol, the network processing of the inner packet headers described above, and verification of the inner packet checksums. Non-IP inner packets are likely to be subject to similar effects.

Protocols that directly consume the payload must have sufficient robustness against misdelivered packets, including ones corrupted in tunnels or corrupted by other use of the zero checksum. That will require an integrity mechanism, and using a standard UDP checksum reduces the computational load in the receiver needed to verify it.

The design for stateful protocols, or protocols where corruption causes cascade effects, requires extra care. In tunnel usage each encapsulating packet provides no function other than transport from tunnel ingress to tunnel egress, so a corruption will commonly affect only the single tunneled packet and not the established protocol state. One common effect is that the inner packet flow sees only a corruption and a misdelivery of the outer packet, which looks like a lost packet.

Some non-tunnel protocols operate with general servers that do not know the source from which they will receive a packet. In such applications a zero UDP checksum is unsuitable, because it is necessary to provide the first level of verification that the packet was intended for the receiving server. Without that verification the server may spend significant resources processing the packet, including sending replies or error messages.

Tunnel protocols that encapsulate IP will generally be safe for deployment, because all IPv4 and IPv6 packets include at least one checksum at either the network or the transport layer, and the network delivery of the inner packet further reduces the effects of corruption. Tunnel protocols carrying non-IP packets may offer equivalent protection when the non-IP networks reduce the risk of misdelivery to applications, but further analysis is necessary for each such protocol.

One unfortunate side effect of the increased use of a zero checksum is that it also increases the likelihood of acceptance when a datagram with a zero UDP checksum is misdelivered. That requires all tunnel protocols using this method to be designed to be robust in the face of misdelivery.
sections.plainLanguage: The change is restricted to tunnels for a reason. A tunnel's own packet has nothing else in it, so a corrupted outer header usually costs one lost packet. A general server, by contrast, needs the checksum to know the datagram was meant for it at all, and would otherwise spend effort answering a packet that was never addressed to it.

sections.title: Middleboxes on the Path
sections.content: RFC 6936 specifies requirements for middleboxes and tunnels that need to traverse middleboxes. Tunnel protocols intending to use a zero UDP checksum need to ensure that they have defined a method for handling cases where a middlebox prevents the path between the tunnel ingress and egress from supporting transmission of datagrams with a zero UDP checksum. This is especially important, because middleboxes that conform to RFC 2460 are likely to discard datagrams with a zero UDP checksum.
sections.plainLanguage: Older firewalls and other middleboxes will simply throw away a UDP packet with no checksum. A tunnel that uses this feature has to notice that and react, and the RFC says so explicitly.

sections.title: The Zero UDP Checksum Update
sections.content:
This specification updates IPv6 to allow a zero UDP checksum in the outer encapsulating datagram of a tunnel protocol. UDP endpoints that implement this update must follow the node requirements in RFC 6936.

The fourth bullet of Section 8.1 of RFC 2460 is deleted. The text that replaces it says that an IPv6 node associates a mode with each used UDP port, for sending and/or receiving packets. Whenever originating a UDP packet for a port in the default mode, an IPv6 node must compute a UDP checksum over the packet and the pseudo-header, and if that computation yields a result of zero the checksum must be changed to hex FFFF for placement in the UDP header, as specified in RFC 2460. IPv6 receivers must by default discard UDP packets containing a zero checksum and should log the error.

As an alternative, certain protocols that use UDP as a tunnel encapsulation may enable zero-checksum mode for a specific port or set of ports for sending and/or receiving. Any node implementing zero-checksum mode must follow the node requirements specified in Section 4 of RFC 6936, and any protocol that enables zero-checksum mode for a specific port or ports must follow the usage requirements specified in Section 5 of RFC 6936. Middleboxes supporting IPv6 must follow requirements 9, 10 and 11 of those usage requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: The change to IPv6 is that a port now has a setting: either the default, where the checksum is computed and a zero checksum is refused, or a special mode that a tunnel protocol may turn on for its own ports. The rest of the IPv6 text is unchanged.

sections.title: Additional Observations
sections.content:
The update was motivated by the existence of a number of protocols being developed in the IETF that are expected to benefit from the change. The RFC makes three further observations.

An empirically based analysis of the probabilities of packet corruption, with or without checksums, has not, to the knowledge of the authors, been conducted since about 2000, and the RFC strongly suggests that a new empirical study be performed, along with extensive analysis of the corruption probabilities of the IPv6 header. That could potentially allow the recommendations in the document to be revised.

A key motivation for the increased use of UDP in tunnelling is a lack of protocol support in middleboxes. New protocols such as LISP may prefer to use UDP tunnels to traverse an end-to-end path successfully and avoid having their packets dropped by middleboxes. If middleboxes were updated to support UDP-Lite of RFC 3828, UDP-Lite would provide better protection than this update offers, and it would be expected to be preferred over this method for many tunnel protocols.

Another issue is that the UDP checksum is overloaded with the task of protecting the IPv6 header for UDP flows, as the TCP checksum is for TCP flows. Protocols that do not use a pseudo-header approach to computing a checksum or CRC have essentially no protection from misdelivered packets.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors note that the measurement of how often packets get corrupted is old, that a lighter alternative to this scheme exists in UDP-Lite and would be better where it is available, and that the IPv6 header has been left unprotected by the design of the checksum in the first place.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Less work is required to generate an attack using a zero UDP checksum than one using a standard full UDP checksum. This does not lead to significant new vulnerabilities, because checksums are not a security measure and can be easily generated by any attacker.

In general, any user of zero UDP checksums should apply the checks and context verification that are possible, to minimize the risk of unintended traffic reaching a particular context. That will not, however, protect against an intentional attack that creates packets with the correct information. Source address validation can help prevent the injection of traffic into contexts by an attacker.

Depending on the hardware design, the processing requirements may differ for tunnels that have a zero UDP checksum and those that calculate one. This processing overhead may need to be considered when deciding whether to enable a tunnel and determining an acceptable rate for transmission. It can become a security risk for designs that can handle significantly more packets with zero UDP checksums than datagrams with a non-zero checksum, such as a tunnel egress. An attacker could try to inject non-zero checksummed UDP packets into a tunnel forwarding zero checksum UDP packets and cause overload in the processing of the non-zero checksums, for example in a router's slow path. Protection mechanisms should therefore be employed where this threat exists. Protection may include source address filtering to prevent an attacker injecting traffic, and throttling the amount of non-zero checksum traffic, which may in turn affect the functioning of the tunnel protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: A checksum is not a security mechanism, so making one easier to produce does not open a real hole. The practical risk is different: if the tunnel is much faster at handling unchecked packets than at handling checked ones, an attacker could flood it with ordinary packets and make it do the slow work. Filtering and rate limiting are the answers.

data.title: New text in RFC 2460
data.code:
An IPv6 node associates a mode with each used UDP port (for sending and/or receiving packets).

Whenever originating a UDP packet for a port in the default mode, an IPv6 node MUST compute a UDP checksum over the packet and the pseudo-header, and, if that computation yields a result of zero, the checksum MUST be changed to hex FFFF for placement in the UDP header, as specified in [RFC2460].  IPv6 receivers MUST by default discard UDP packets containing a zero checksum and SHOULD log the error.

As an alternative, certain protocols that use UDP as a tunnel encapsulation MAY enable zero-checksum mode for a specific port (or set of ports) for sending and/or receiving.
